message.content:
You are running a design finish review on a five-slide PowerPoint deck. You did not build it and must not assume the builder's framing was right. Be specific and hard to please; vague praise is worthless.

CONTEXT. The user has a "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" series for Baylor Athletics Applied Performance. Five decks already exist in one composition, and the user said "all the slides look good but they look the same." A single slide (sheet 3) was redesigned as an engineering shop drawing and passed its own review. The user then said: roll that look out to all five slides of the Data to Decision deck. That rollout is what you are reviewing. Sheet 3 has already been reviewed and fixed — review it only for how it sits in the set, not from scratch.

FIXED CONSTRAINTS (the department's, not negotiable):
- Palette: forest #0B2A1F, Baylor green #154734, mid green #1E6349, Baylor gold #FFB81C (DARK grounds only — 1.7:1 on bone), antique gold #9A8033 (light-ground gold and hairlines), pale mint #AFD2C0 (secondary text on dark, ~9:1), mint surface #E4F0E9, bone #F4F2EC (light ground), gray-green #4E5150 (LIGHT grounds only).
- Type: DIN Pro, DIN Pro Light, DIN Pro Cond, DIN Pro Cond Medium. The "Baylor Bears Font" display face is allowed exactly ONCE per deck and only on slide 1.
- Contrast floor 3.0:1 for text against its containing shape.
- Slides MUST alternate dark / light / dark / light / dark. This is enforced by the repo's own QA.
- Gold accent cap: 2 objects per slide.

PRODUCT TRUTH:
- Audience: cross-functional Baylor Health & Wellness staff (S&C, athletic medicine, sport science, nutrition, mental health), presented to as peers, several of whom know their discipline better than the presenter. Anything overstated gets caught by name in the room.
- Scene: a staff meeting, five minutes on the agenda between operational items, projector, mixed lighting, people half-turned in chairs. The deck has to earn the next four minutes in the first fifteen seconds.
- Format: hook, problem, insight, application, takeaway. Surface-level by design: awareness plus one takeaway, not mastery.
- Every number traces to a source. The 3.0 % coefficient of variation and ICC 0.96 are from Rebelo et al., Sports Medicine 2026. "±1 SD" is that paper's own example of a sensitive setting, not a standard. The −2.0 % and −6.0 % readings are ILLUSTRATIVE and must be labelled so.
- Doctrine: establish the noise floor before claiming a change is meaningful; prefer within-athlete framing; Applied Performance supplies evidence and does NOT clear athletes to play; decoration must not imply more certainty than the evidence supports.
- A stated product risk: "five decks that feel like five fills of one template" is a failure mode. So is "a deck that looks like a vendor pitch" — this is a colleague talking, not a company selling.

THE DIRECTION CONTRACT the build committed to (judge the render against it):
- THESIS: a five-minute argument is a set of drawings, not a set of headlines. Every sheet dimensions its evidence the way a shop drawing dimensions a part, so the room reads a measurement before it reads a claim. Refuses the category default — a title over a picture over a caption — on all five sheets, not just the one with a chart.
- OWN-WORLD: a drawing set issued two ways. Odd sheets are blueprint (forest ground, mint linework, Baylor gold). Even sheets are whiteprint (bone ground, green linework, antique gold). Both carry the same frame, the same 45° section hatch, the same condensed all-caps annotation, the same ruled notes row and three-cell title block. Recognisable with every word removed.
- STORY: the room opens a drawing set — the question on the cover, the measured problem on sheet 2, the noise floor dimensioned on sheet 3, the schedule of what changes on sheet 4, one line to carry out on sheet 5.
- FIRST VIEWPORT: sheet 1 is a cover — display line at plan scale on the left, scope and audience ruled into cells on the right, the drawing's name in the title block.

WHAT TO INSPECT (read every image):
1. /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Education_Content_Agent/.claude/worktrees/design-variants/preview-sd/sheet1.svg.png
2. .../preview-sd/sheet2.svg.png
3. .../preview-sd/sheet3.svg.png
4. .../preview-sd/sheet4.svg.png
5. .../preview-sd/sheet5.svg.png
(all under /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Education_Content_Agent/.claude/worktrees/design-variants/)
Each is a 16:9 slide letterboxed into a square canvas — the dark grey bands top and bottom are padding, not part of the slide.
6. The whole set at once: .../decks-out/design-studies/Data_to_Decision_ShopDrawing_contact.png (2-column contact sheet, sheets 1-5 reading left-to-right then down; the bottom-right cell is empty).
7. Source: .../decks/variants/shop-drawing.js
8. The narrative it must carry faithfully: .../decks/data-to-decision.js — check nothing meaningful was dropped, reworded into a different claim, or invented. Pay attention to whether any note text on a sheet is authored by the kit rather than drawn from the deck, and whether that authored text asserts anything the deck does not.
9. The quality floor: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/impeccable/reference/craft-floor.md — read it and apply it.

Note: these renders come from a small in-house SVG renderer, so text metrics are approximate and run WIDE. Judge composition, hierarchy, colour, spacing, pacing across the set, and legibility at projector distance. Do NOT report kerning or exact line-break differences as defects. DO report text that visibly collides with a rule or another block.

RETURN exactly these six sections, nothing else:
1. VERDICT — one word: pass, pass-with-fixes, or rebuild.
2. CONTRACT AUDIT — for each of THESIS / OWN-WORLD / STORY / FIRST VIEWPORT, does the set keep it? Say where it does not.
3. SET COHERENCE — does this read as one drawing set or as five fills of one template? Is the blueprint/whiteprint alternation carrying real meaning or is it decoration? Is the pacing right across five sheets (density, quiet, where the weight falls)? Name the weakest sheet and why.
4. MATERIAL FINDINGS — numbered, most severe first. Each: what is wrong, which sheet and where, why it matters to THIS room, and the specific fix. Only things that change what a viewer understands or whether they can read it. If none, say so plainly.
5. TRUTH CHECK — any claim, number, or visual that overstates the evidence; any illustrative figure not labelled; any kit-authored sentence that asserts more than the deck's own source material supports.
6. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE — what is working, so a fix pass does not sand it off.

    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])

    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)

Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.
    - mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute and mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file for file writes → these run code in a subprocess and discard the sandbox FS; they are for analysis, processing, and computation only.
  </when_not_to_use>

    File writes use the native Write or Edit tool — mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute, mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file, and Bash subprocesses do not persist edits to the host filesystem.
    Applies to all file types: code, configs, plans, specs, YAML, JSON, markdown.
  </file_writing_policy>

  <output_constraints>
    <artifact_policy>
      Write artifacts (code, configs, PRDs) to files. Return only: file path + 1-line description.
    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>

If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.

content.content:
# Craft floor

Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.

## Verify

Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in the batched inspection rounds, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.

- **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
- **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
- **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
- **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
- **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
- **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
- **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
- **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.

## Refuse

These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.

Page scaffolds:

- Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
- The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
- A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
- A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.

Surface habits:

- Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
- Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
- A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
- Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
- Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
- Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
- A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
- Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
- Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.

The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.
=========== DECK ===========
/**
 * Data to Decision — narrative from briefs/2026-08-18-data-to-decision.md.
 * Every number here traces to that brief. Do not add one that does not.
 */

module.exports = {
  slug: "Data_to_Decision",
  title: "Data to Decision",
  topic: "Data to Decision",
  coreQuestion: "Before a number changes a training plan, how do we know it moved for a reason?",

  hook: {
    display: "THE NUMBER",
    accent: "MOVED.",
    sub: "Every dashboard in this building is very good at telling you a value changed.\nNone of them can tell you whether it changed for a reason.",
    notes: [
      "~45 sec.",
      "",
      "Open by asking the room: hands up if a number on a screen has ever changed what you did that week.",
      "Most hands go up. Good — that is the behaviour we are examining, not criticising.",
      "",
      "Frame it as cross-functional straight away: this is not a sport science problem. Anyone",
      "who repeats a measurement — a strength test, a wellness score, a range-of-motion check —",
      "has the same problem.",
      "",
      "Do not say 'noise floor' yet. That is slide 3.",
    ].join("\n"),
  },

  problem: {
    head: "A red cell is not an instruction",
    body: [
      "Monitoring software reports values. It does not know the error of the test that produced them,",
      "and it cannot tell a real change from the ordinary variation of running the same test twice.",
      "",
      "The deeper habit is worse: we treat 'meaningful' and 'statistically significant' as the same word.",
      "For one athlete they are not. Group-derived thresholds lack the resolution to guide day-to-day",
      "decisions for an individual. That is Rebelo and colleagues, not my paraphrase.",
    ].join(" "),
    stat: "3.0%",
    statCaption: "Coefficient of variation for a well-regarded fatigue protocol — ICC 0.96. A 2% change on that test is not a change.",
    notes: [
      "~60 sec.",
      "",
      "The stat is the anchor. Say it plainly: this is one of the good tests. An ICC of 0.96 is about",
      "as reliable as applied testing gets. And it still carries 3% of measurement noise.",
      "",
      "So when someone shows you a 2% drop on that test and asks what to do about it — the honest",
      "answer is that nothing has been observed yet.",
      "",
      "Expect the room to get slightly uncomfortable here. That is the point of the slide.",
      "Do not resolve it yet.",
      "",
      "Source: Rebelo et al., Sports Medicine 2026.",
    ].join("\n"),
  },

  insight: {
    head: "First the noise floor. Then the decision.",
    visual: (v) =>
      v.band({
        label: "typical error of the test",
        inside: "Inside the band\nIndistinguishable from running\nthe test twice. Acting here is a\nfalse positive with a real cost.",
        outside: "Clears the band\nNow ask the second question:\nis it big enough to be worth\nacting on for this athlete?",
        // For directions that draw the band as a dimensioned tolerance. The editorial
        // and split-field kits read none of these, so they cost those builds nothing.
        typicalError: 3.0,
        errorNote: "CV 3.0 % of the protocol · ICC 0.96",
        source: "Rebelo et al., Sports Medicine 2026.",
        readings: [
          { id: "B", pct: -6.0, state: "outside" },
          { id: "A", pct: -2.0, state: "inside" },
        ],
      }),
    foot: "There are two ways to be wrong and they do not cost the same. Call a change real when it is not, and you have made a training change nobody needed. Miss a real one, and an at-risk athlete keeps training. Which mistake costs more is what should set your threshold. The paper offers ±1 SD as one example of a sensitive setting, not as a standard.",
    notes: [
      "~75 sec. If they retain one slide, make it this one.",
      "",
      "Walk the band left to right. The band is the test's own error. Anything inside it is noise.",
      "",
      "Then the move that makes this useful — the threshold is a DECISION, not a statistic.",
      "Quote it directly: 'the tolerance for error must align with the athlete's performance",
      "environment.' Where missing early maladaptation is the costlier mistake, the framework",
      "explicitly supports a MORE sensitive threshold — plus or minus 1 SD — accepting more false",
      "alarms on purpose.",
      "",
      "And the counter-case, which matters in this room: returning to play from injury is where",
      "clarity is paramount, so the threshold goes the other way. Same data, different threshold,",
      "because the cost of each error is different.",
      "",
      "If you only land one sentence today, land that one.",
      "",
      "Source: Rebelo et al., Sports Medicine 2026.",
    ].join("\n"),
  },

  apply: {
    head: "Three questions, in this order",
    columns: [
      { who: "Strength & Conditioning", what: "Before changing a programme off a monitoring flag, ask what that test's typical error is. A 2% drop on a 3% CV test is not a drop." },
      { who: "Athletic Medicine", what: "Return to play is the case where the source favours the conservative threshold. We supply evidence; the clearance decision is yours." },
      { who: "Nutrition & Mental Health", what: "The same three questions apply to any repeated measure, including subjective ones. A wellness score has a noise floor too." },
      { who: "Sport Science", what: "Our job is to publish the error next to the number. A dashboard showing a value without its error is asking the room to guess." },
    ],
    rule: "Typical error first. Then whether the change beats it. Then whether it is worth acting on, and which mistake would cost more.",
    notes: [
      "~60 sec.",
      "",
      "The order is the whole point. Everyone's instinct is to start at question three — is this",
      "bad? — and question one is the one that actually gates the decision.",
      "",
      "Be honest about our own position when you get to the Sport Science column: for most of our",
      "tests we have not established the typical error. That is not an excuse, it is the first task,",
      "and it is finite work.",
      "",
      "If someone asks 'so what IS our typical error for CMJ' — the correct answer is 'we don't know",
      "yet, and that is the most useful thing I can tell you today.'",
    ].join("\n"),
  },

  takeaway: {
    oneThing: "A number is only a signal once it clears the noise of its own measurement — and the threshold you set should be chosen by the cost of being wrong.",
    question: "Pick one number you already act on. Do you know its typical error? If not, what would it take to find out?",
    notes: [
      "~45 sec.",
      "",
      "Land the one thing, then hand the room the question and stop talking.",
      "",
      "The follow-up conversation you want: someone naming a specific test they want the noise",
      "floor for. That is a concrete piece of work and it is how this becomes real rather than",
      "a nice idea.",
      "",
      "Two things they will push on, and what I would say:",
      "",
      "'This is a reason to never act on anything.' — The opposite. Where missing maladaptation",
      "costs more, the framework supports a MORE sensitive threshold on purpose. The point is",
      "choosing deliberately rather than inheriting what the software shipped with.",
      "",
      "'Do we know the typical error for our tests?' — For most, no. Say so.",
    ].join("\n"),
  },
};

      "And the counter-case, which matters in this room: returning to play from injury is where",
      "clarity is paramount, so the threshold goes the other way. Same data, different threshold,",
      "because the cost of each error is different.",
      "",
      "If you only land one sentence today, land that one.",
      "",
      "Source: Rebelo et al., Sports Medicine 2026.",
    ].join("\n"),
  },

  apply: {
    head: "Three questions, in this order",
    columns: [
      { who: "Strength & Conditioning", what: "Before changing a programme off a monitoring flag, ask what that test's typical error is. A 2% drop on a 3% CV test is not a drop." },
      { who: "Athletic Medicine", what: "Return to play is the case where the source favours the conservative threshold. We supply evidence; the clearance decision is yours." },
      { who: "Nutrition & Mental Health", what: "The same three questions apply to any repeated measure, including subjective ones. A wellness score has a noise floor too." },
      { who: "Sport Science", what: "Our job is to publish the error next to the number. A dashboard showing a value without its error is asking the room to guess." },
    ],
    rule: "Typical error first. Then whether the change beats it. Then whether it is worth acting on, and which mistake would cost more.",
    notes: [
      "~60 sec.",
      "",
      "The order is the whole point. Everyone's instinct is to start at question three — is this",
      "bad? — and question one is the one that actually gates the decision.",
      "",
      "Be honest about our own position when you get to the Sport Science column: for most of our",
      "tests we have not established the typical error. That is not an excuse, it is the first task,",
      "and it is finite work.",
      "",
      "If someone asks 'so what IS our typical error for CMJ' — the correct answer is 'we don't know",
      "yet, and that is the most useful thing I can tell you today.'",
    ].join("\n"),
  },

  takeaway: {
    oneThing: "A number is only a signal once it clears the noise of its own measurement — and the threshold you set should be chosen by the cost of being wrong.",
    question: "Pick one number you already act on. Do you know its typical error? If not, what would it take to find out?",
    notes: [
      "~45 sec.",
      "",
      "Land the one thing, then hand the room the question and stop talking.",
      "",
      "The follow-up conversation you want: someone naming a specific test they want the noise",
      "floor for. That is a concrete piece of work and it is how this becomes real rather than",
      "a nice idea.",
      "",
      "Two things they will push on, and what I would say:",
      "",
      "'This is a reason to never act on anything.' — The opposite. Where missing maladaptation",
      "costs more, the framework supports a MORE sensitive threshold on purpose. The point is",
      "choosing deliberately rather than inheriting what the software shipped with.",
      "",
      "'Do we know the typical error for our tests?' — For most, no. Say so.",
    ].join("\n"),
  },
};
